new_entities.name: Mouth taping during sleep
new_entities.description: Sealing or closing the mouth during sleep to encourage nasal breathing and potentially reduce snoring or sleep-disordered breathing.

new_entities.name: Sleep apnea outcomes
new_entities.description: Outcomes related to obstructive sleep apnea severity, airflow, and related sleep-breathing measures.

edges.effect_quant: In a 2024 nonrandomized clinical trial of 54 patients with OSA, mouth closure increased total inspiratory flow overall by 1.0 L/min but worsened airflow by 1.9 L/min in the subgroup with the greatest baseline mouth breathing; a 2022 preliminary study in 20 mouth-breathers with mild OSA reported median AHI improvement from 8.3 to 4.7 events/h with mouth taping.
edges.population: adults with mouth breathing, snoring, or obstructive sleep apnea using mouth closure or taping during sleep
edges.mechanism: Mouth closure may reduce oral-route breathing and improve some airflow patterns, but in patients who rely on the mouth to bypass nasal or velopharyngeal obstruction it can also worsen airflow and obstructive physiology.
edges.summary: Mouth taping is not a one-directional 'biohack win.' Some mild or selected mouth-breathing patients may improve, but responses are heterogeneous and patients with significant upstream obstruction may worsen when forced into nasal-only airflow.
edges.caveats: Do not generalize small-study improvements to all patients with OSA. The safety profile depends heavily on airway anatomy, disease severity, and whether mouth breathing is compensatory rather than purely dysfunctional.

evidence.citation: Yang H et al 2024 JAMA Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg
evidence.notes: Mouth Closure and Airflow in Patients With Obstructive Sleep Apnea: A Nonrandomized Clinical Trial.

evidence.notes: Mouth Puffing Phenomenon and Upper Airway Features May Be Used to Predict the Severity of Obstructive Sleep Apnea.
